title_en: From ancient Asia to the AI age: Has China’s ‘beauty stratagem’ found a new victim in Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
excerpt_en: ‘Honey traps’ have long been used to gain an advantage over a rival. In China, it is a tactic documented in stories that go back 2 millennia.
body_en: Jensen Huang: in the spotlight and out of a job. Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images Extramarital activities have led to the resignation of one of America’s most influential tech bosses, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The saga has also raised the specter of an age-old spying tactic: the “honey trap.”

Huang stepped down following media reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence agencies. She previously worked for Megaspeed, a cloud computing company under U.S. scrutiny for allegedly helping China obtain restricted AI chips.
Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair. And amid reports of a second with a company executive who reports to him, he tendered his resignation to the Nvidia board on Nov. 12, 2026.

The sensitivity of Huang’s work – AI is increasingly seen as central to national security – has turned a company matter into an international issue. China’s Foreign Ministry has denied the espionage allegations and accused the U.S. of “fabricating so-called spy narratives and ⁠⁠⁠⁠using them as a pretext for imposing ⁠⁠⁠⁠a technological blockade.” Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets have been leaked.
Yet part of what makes the accusations so believable is history is dotted with examples of men being distracted, compromised or spied on by attractive men and women deployed for that purpose.
Indeed, in China it recalls an ancient political tactic known as “meiren ji” or the “ beauty stratagem.”

As a scholar specializing in U.S.-China relations, I believe that regardless of the particulars of the Huang case, the political logic behind the beauty stratagem – using personal relationships to obtain information, influence decisions and weaken opponents – remains relevant today. As such, it would be no surprise if the tactic was being used amid the growing U.S.-China competition over AI and advanced semiconductors.

The beauty stratagem of Ancient China “Meiren ji” is one of “ Thirty-Six Stratagems,” a Chinese military text of uncertain origin but generally believed to have derived from oral and written histories from the Warring States period — 475–221 BCE. Its 31st stratagem states that personal relationships can be used to influence political opponents and recommends exploiting an adversary’s personal desires and emotional vulnerabilities to weaken their judgment and undermine their leadership.
The “Thirty-Six Stratagems” is both a playbook for warfare and a reflection on past experience.
Indeed, one of China’s most famous beauty stratagem stories dates back more than 2,000 years to the Spring and Autumn period of Chinese history.

In the fifth century BCE, King Goujian of Yue, in modern-day southern China, was defeated by King Fuchai of Wu, its northern neighbor, and forced to submit. But Goujian secretly rebuilt his strength and prepared for revenge.
According to the ancient historical text “ Wu Yue Chun Qiu,” Yue sent two beautiful women – Xi Shi and Zheng Dan – to Fuchai, hoping he would become distracted by pleasure and neglect state affairs.
The plan reportedly worked. Fuchai, seemingly enchanted by the beautiful women, gradually ignored Yue’s threat. Meanwhile, Goujian prepared for war and in 473 BCE Yue conquered Wu.

A 19th-century etching depicting Zheng Dan and Xi Shi. Wikimedia Commons Xi Shi’s actual role in Wu’s downfall remains unclear. Wu’s defeat involved poor political decisions and Yue’s military recovery.
Still, the story illustrated an important idea in Chinese political strategy: exploiting an opponent’s personal weaknesses can sometimes be more effective than confronting him directly.
A similar tactic appears in the 14th-century novel “ Romance of the Three Kingdoms,” considered one of the classics of Chinese literature.

It tells the story of Dong Zhuo, a powerful warlord who controlled the imperial court during the late Eastern Han Dynasty. To remove him, Wang Yun, a senior court official loyal to the Han Dynasty promised a beautiful young woman, named Diaochan, in marriage to Dong Zhuo’s military commander. He then offered the same woman to Dong Zhuo.

The scheme fueled jealousy and distrust between the two men, eventually enabling Wang Yun to persuade Dong Zhuo’s underling to kill him. Wang Yun then briefly took charge of the imperial court on behalf of the Han emperor.

The ‘honey trap’ of modern spyware In modern intelligence operations, using romantic or sexual relationships to approach targets, obtain sensitive information or exert influence is commonly called a “ honey trap.” It is, moreover, certainly not unique to China. Western and Soviet intelligence agencies used intimate relationships for espionage frequently during the Cold War.

Modern China also has documented cases. One example involves French diplomat Bernard Boursicot and the Chinese opera performer Shi Pei Pu. The pair met in Beijing in 1964 and maintained a long-term intimate relationship. Throughout, Boursicot was providing French diplomatic documents to China. The spying was eventually exposed and both involved were prosecuted for espionage in France in the 1980s.

Bernard Boursicot and Shi Pei Pu in the dock during an espionage trial in Paris in May 1986. Laurent Maous/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images A more recent example involves former U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell and Christine Fang, a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Swalwell acknowledged in 2015 that he had been physically intimate with Fang on several occasions. At the time, Fang helped raise funds for Swalwell’s campaign and helped place an intern in his congressional office.

Why Jensen Huang is strategically important Jensen Huang’s position would make him a prime target for such a “honey trap” operation. His company has become central to the technological competition between the U.S and China. As AI becomes increasingly important to economic development, military capabilities and national security, moreover, Washington has repeatedly tightened restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China, hoping to slow its access to computing power.

title_en: Who is Colette Kress, interim Nvidia CEO after Jensen Huang exit?
excerpt_en: Chief financial officer, reportedly disparaged by Huang during summer meeting, to take over on short-term basis
body_en: The hunt is on for a new Nvidia CEO. It comes after a whirlwind week, which saw the company head and co-founder, Jensen Huang, resign amid multiple allegations of extramarital affairs, including one that involved an alleged Chinese spy and two with company employees.

Nvidia immediately named Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as the interim CEO. It’s possible she could stay on permanently, but the company could also name another candidate for the full-time role. Names that have been floated include Ian Buck, who manages Nvidia’s AI hardware and software products, and Rene Haas, a former Nvidia employee and the current CEO of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker.
Related: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after alleged affairs

Whoever takes over from Huang will have tremendous sway in the burgeoning world of artificial intelligence. The entire AI ecosphere relies on Nvidia, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Nvidia is also a central driver of the US economy and one of the world’s most valuable companies, with a market cap of around $4tn.

Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993, is known as an ambitious and visionary CEO who had a hand in most all aspects of the business. He led in an unusual management style, having about 60 direct reports, giving him more control over the company’s daily functions. His son and daughter also work at Nvidia, with his daughter seen as his possible proxy, but neither appear to have sufficient experience to take the helm.

Kress, 59, joined Nvidia in 2013 as the CFO after working in finance roles at Texas Instruments, Microsoft and Cisco. She’s a regular contributor to the company’s quarterly earnings calls, and has overseen Nvidia go from a niche firm geared toward video game chips to a trillion-dollar AI juggernaut. People who know her describe Kress as a calming contrast to Huang’s often confrontational style, Reuters reported.

“Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” Harvey C Jones, the newly named chair of Nvidia’s board of directors, said in a statement on Thursday. “The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team.”

But that sentiment may not be shared by Huang. During a meeting this past summer, the CEO said Kress was “a deer in the headlights” and interrupted her presentation, a person familiar with the comments told the Wall Street Journal. Huang insinuated during that August meeting that Kress was not someone who could help him make decisions.
However, Kress praised Huang in a memo to employees on Thursday, saying she would continue “building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years”.
Many investors, analysts and industry sources who spoke to Reuters questioned whether a finance executive could preserve the technological risk-taking that turned Nvidia into an AI chips powerhouse.

“Putting [Kress] in the interim role makes sense to keep the markets calm, but I don’t think she is the long-term visionary that Nvidia needs to continue its current trajectory,” said Anshel Sag, principal analyst at Moor Insights and Strategy.
Kress, who said in her memo that Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people”, will serve as both the CEO and interim CFO until the board names a permanent successor.

The board said it was starting a search for Huang’s permanent replacement and is considering internal and external candidates. Along with Kress, Buck is seen as a possible successor. He has worked at Nvidia since 2004 and in charge of deploying generative AI in partnership with the world’s top AI companies, including Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, OpenAI and more.

Haas, the CEO of Arm Holdings, is also well-known at Nvidia, having worked there for seven years as a vice president and general manager before joining Arm in 2013. Lisa Su, the CEO of chipmaker AMD, is also being named as a possible replacement for Huang. Her company is Nvidia’s most direct and fierce competitor; she’s also a distant cousin to Huang.

Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation, said Kress could face congressional questions about the company’s oversight of chip sales involving Chinese military-linked institutions and south-east Asian intermediaries.
In a 2023 interview with an Israeli publication, Kress credited her two young sons with urging her to join Nvidia in 2013 because they knew its chips from their video games.

She became a billionaire in 2025 based on the value of her Nvidia equity, according to media reports, and Forbes said her net worth of $1.2 billion in mid-2026 put her in 32nd place on its list of America’s richest self-made women.
Kress, who holds an undergraduate degree in finance and an MBA, was also named among the 50 most powerful women in business on rankings compiled by Fortune and Forbes magazines in recent years.
Nvidia’s CEO turmoil comes as the company is set to report its third-quarter earnings next Tuesday.

title_en: ‘Even a snail would agree’: Greta Thunberg ridicules Australia’s slow climate action
excerpt_en: Comments came as Indigenous activist Rikki Dank urged the Australian PM to heed the calls for action on climate change
body_en: An Indigenous climate activist who is taking the Australian government to the UN human rights committee over its coal and gas exports stood alongside Greta Thunberg at the Cop summit to demand Anthony Albanese “stop speaking and start listening.”

Draped in traditional dress in front of a media throng, Rikki Dank, a Gudanji and Wakaya traditional owner, delivered an impassioned plea to Albanese to listen to “the Australian people when they say no more new coal, oil and gas”.
Related: ‘I was home alone when the glacier collapsed. My mum called and told me to run’ – This is climate breakdown
Albanese on Thursday defended his major speech at the opening of Cop31 after facing criticism for omitting the phrase “fossil fuels”.

Australia is the president of the two-week negotiations at Cop31 being held in Antalya, Turkey. A key push from the two hosts is to garner support for a “35 by 35” pledge for 35% of end-use energy to be from electricity by the year 2035.

The UN secretary general, António Guterres, and several countries are pushing the two hosts to also progress a proposal from last year’s Cop president, Brazil, to have countries develop roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels.

Squeezed into a corner of the vast Cop31 media centre, Thunberg was flanked by Dank and other climate advocates, including a Nepalese MP who had helped rescue people from a landslide that followed an August glacier collapse that killed more than 1,500 people.
Thunberg said: “It is more clear than ever in spaces like these that the situation could not be less under control. The planet is not dying, it is being killed.
“And we know by who. And it is being killed by the very same people often thought to come to our rescue.”
Asked whether she agreed with comments about Australia’s slow record on climate action, Thunberg told the crowd: “Even a snail would agree with that.
“It’s common sense. It doesn’t get more clear than that.”
When asked for his reaction to Thunberg’s comments, Albanese sought to highlight Australia’s climate credentials instead.
“Well, I haven’t seen it, but she’s entitled to her views,'” the prime minister said.
“What we are doing is putting forward practical plans to achieve a considerable decrease.”

‘Drinking water poisoned’ Dank is one of 10 Australians behind a complaint before the UN human rights committee – known as the Hard Truths case – that claims the Australian government has failed to protect them from climate pollution, including from its vast exports of coal and LNG that are among the highest in the world.

Lawyers behind the case are hoping for a resolution in the next 18 months. While a committee declaration is not legally binding, a negative finding would be a major embarrassment and would carry significant political weight.
“My Country is being fracked, our drinking water poisoned and our history erased as we speak,” Dank said.

She said the prime minister “needs to stop speaking and start listening to our brothers and sisters across the world when they say they don’t want us to export coal, oil or gas and the climate harms that they bring with them”.
Related: Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?
Albanese had a series of bi-lateral meetings on the sidelines of Cop31 on Thursday with Bangladesh, Lebanon, Pacific leaders and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham.
He was criticised for a set-piece six-minute speech on Wednesday that did not use the term “fossil fuels.”
Albanese said: “You could pick out any number of things that were not in what was a short speech.”

title_en: Second world war ‘brain’ bunker in cliffs of Dover opens to public
excerpt_en: The bunker, entered via a hatch in a field, controlled a gun battery used to attack German ships in Channel
body_en: It has been kept secret for decades, buried four metres deep into the white cliffs of Dover. But from Friday, members of the public will finally be able to visit a pioneering command bunker that was ordered by Winston Churchill and proved a vital defence during the second world war.

The Fan Bay plotting room, which is encased in concrete, housed the first land-based computer-aided targeting system. This acted as a “brain” for a gun battery that was used to defend Dover and attack German ships in the Channel, according to Jon Stewart, who led the excavation project for the National Trust.
Stewart was the first person to enter the bunker when it was rediscovered in 2017 after it had been secretly mothballed in 1957 and classified until 1981 owing to its military importance.

“It was a Tutankhamun moment for a conflict archaeologist,” he said. “We had done all this research on the people who had served there, and then suddenly you’re standing in their office. It was an exciting moment.”

The plotting room and the artillery it controlled can be directly traced to Churchill. Soon after his “fight them on the beaches” speech, he visited the Kent coast and was alarmed to observe enemy ships passing through the strait of Dover unchallenged.
At the same time, Dover was on the frontline of a Britain facing regular bombardment by enemy guns in occupied France.
In a July 1940 memo Churchill wrote: “We have to fight for command of the straits by artillery, to destroy the enemy batteries and fortify our own.”

He ordered the most advanced technology to be used and demanded weekly updates on progress on Dover’s new defences. The guns were ready within 100 days and the plotting room bunker was completed 64 days later.
“The guns were known around here as Churchill’s pets,” Stewart said.

Physical traces of the urgency of the construction were still visible at the site, said Stewart. He pointed to the rough openings through the walls and floors for the cabling. Contemporary accounts describe how the equipment was installed before drawings governing its layout were available.

The plotting room housed a 1.8-metre-long electromechanical computer known as a fire direction table. It was used to calculate the position of moving ships when shells hit and to send firing instructions to gun crews.

Stewart said the discovery of the plotting room reminded him of the rescue of Bletchley Park, the codebreaking site in Buckinghamshire, in the 1990s. “We didn’t know about it then, but now it’s all part of our national consciousness,” he said. “The plotting room is a new hidden history.”

He added: “We tend to think of plotting tables as glamorous Wrens [members of the Women’s Royal Naval Service] pushing around markers on a map as they do in war films. But it’s not a map – it’s a really cutting edge electromechanical computer, and it is completely unique.”
The computer was deliberately destroyed in 1957 to stop it falling into enemy hands.
Up to 10 people at a time worked in the plotting room. Stewart is keen to make contact with anyone who had family members who served there, to help him understand how the machine worked.
“What we know about it is based on a manual and ghost markings on the floor. I would really love to hear if anybody knows if their family members served at Fan Bay because the records are scant.”

The identities of only a handful of people who operated the computer are known. They include Wallas Eaton, an actor who later appeared as Senator Ludicrus Sextus in the TV comedy series Up Pompeii, alongside Frankie Howerd.
A man named WP Bryant, a lance bombardier, was also recorded as a plotter at Fan Bay. “He was a tailor so he probably had a head for numbers,” said Stewart.

The plotting room, which from Friday can be visited via National Trust guided tours through a hatch in a field, has been preserved as Stewart and his team found it. Remnants include old newspapers found on the floor, old shoes and official notices. There is also chalked graffiti on one of the service tunnels saying “heroes fan hole Dodds and Petitt”. Stewart said Dodds and Petitt may have been involved in installing cables to the bunker.
“They were probably self-appointed heroes responsible for marshalling horrible thick cable through particularly uncomfortable tunnels,” he said.

“There’s something very special about standing in a place that has changed so little since the people who worked here left. Rather than recreate the past, we’ve carefully conserved the plotting room so visitors can experience it much as we found it, with all the marks of its history still visible. It’s a rare opportunity to discover a completely different side of the white cliffs.”

title_en: More Than Numbers: Portraits of U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
excerpt_en: The post More Than Numbers: Portraits of U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: The Department of Homeland Security says it’s not detaining Americans.
In written statements, it has said that “allegations that ICE is arresting and deporting U.S. citizens is FALSE.”

It has said that “when individuals are briefly questioned under ‘reasonable suspicion’ and are found to be U.S. citizens, they are immediately released.” And it has said that “U.S. citizen agitators are only held while they actively remain a safety threat to our officers and the public.”
But ProPublica has identified more than 500 citizens detained since President Donald Trump returned to office.

Among them is an elderly car wash owner whom agents repeatedly knocked to the ground as they detained several of his workers. A 6-year-old whose mother says still has nightmares after agents pointed guns at him and his siblings. A high school senior who was detained after she tried to stop officers from questioning her autistic younger brother. A dad who was held for several days and missed his daughter’s third birthday.
Over the past year, several of these people shared the lingering effects of what happened to them with ProPublica.
Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan In their own neighborhood Photographed at their home in a Boston suburb “We have so much trauma just from the 30 minutes we were held.”

Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan In September 2025, Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan learned that ICE agents had intercepted members of her family as they drove one of her uncles to a court hearing. Ramirez Sanan, then 17, said she rushed to the scene and discovered agents had broken the car windows and pulled her two uncles, her mother and her younger brother out. Video of the incident showed agents kicking and slamming Ramirez Sanan’s mother to the ground and then twisting her arms to handcuff her. Ramirez Sanan said she saw other agents questioning her brother against a fence, threatening to arrest him if he couldn’t prove he had legal status.

“Him being a 13-year-old with autism, he doesn’t understand these things like we do. He didn’t know what ‘a legal status’ is. He’s not able to tell them: ‘Yes, I have a legal status. I’m born here,’” Ramirez Sanan said. She said that when she rushed toward her mom and brother, begging agents to let them go, they detained her. “It was really scary thinking that they might have taken us and deported us to Guatemala, where we don’t have anything.”

DHS said that its agents intercepted the car in order to detain the uncle who was going to court that day, and that they “used the appropriate force necessary.” He was facing charges of sexual assault on a child and remains in ICE custody. He has pleaded not guilty.

As for Ramirez Sanan, her mother and her brother, they were released the day of the incident. Her mother, who has lived in the United States for 20 years and has a green card, was treated at a hospital for a concussion, bruising and nerve damage in one of her arms.

“We have so much trauma just from the 30 minutes we were held,” said Ramirez Sanan, who struggled with anxiety and depression after the incident. “I lost my whole senior year fighting this. My brother isn’t the same either.”

Andrea Velez On her way to work Photographed in Los Angeles In June 2025, Andrea Velez was dropped off at work at a shoe company in downtown Los Angeles and inadvertently walked into an immigration raid on street vendors. She said one of the masked agents rushed toward her, grabbed her and slammed her to the pavement. Velez said she attempted to shield herself with her work bag.

“Throughout the whole time, I kept saying I was a U.S. citizen,” Velez recalled, saying that agents called her an “alleged U.S. citizen” even after they checked her ID. “They kept saying how many ‘bodies they got’ that day.”

Velez said that she was detained for two days, and that she was denied an opportunity to call family or a lawyer for most of that time. The government charged Velez with assault. DHS said she “made physical contact” with agents and tried to impede them. A judge ultimately dismissed the case.
After her arrest, Velez said she was so afraid of being detained again that she worked remotely and avoided going outside.

Quentin Williams At the end of his school day as a teaching assistant Photographed in Inver Grove Heights, Minnesota In January, not long after immigration agents in Minneapolis had shot and killed an American woman named Renee Good, Quentin Williams, a teaching assistant at nearby Roosevelt High School, was guiding students toward buses when more agents arrived outside his building.
Williams said that agents began confronting students and staff. At some point during the commotion, he said, the agents threw him to the ground and choked him so hard he couldn’t breathe.
“They didn’t even know what they were doing — just kind of being reckless [with] assault rifles out and pepper-spraying staff after they took me down,” Williams recalled.
Agents drove Williams to the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building, where they detained him for several hours.

Later, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi published his photo on her social media accounts, describing him as a “Minnesota rioter.” Federal authorities issued a warrant for his arrest for assaulting officers. The charges against him were eventually dismissed, and he’s filed a claim against the government for damages over his arrest.

title_en: Home sales hit 16-year low in October amid record-high mortgage rates
excerpt_en: Sales of built units fell to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, with mortgage rates at nearly three-year high
body_en: US existing home sales hit a 16-year low in October as buyers were driven away by record-high mortgage rates and rising inflation, according to new data released on Wednesday.

Sales of already built units dropped to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, the National Association of Realtors (NAR) reported. The median existing-home sales price increased slightly to $416,700. Declines in sales were seen in the midwest, south and west, though sales in the north-east held steady.

Mortgage rates had been steadily declining in 2024 and 2025, with the 30-year rate falling below 6% for the first time in February 2026. But increasing inflation and higher interest rates amid the Iran war have pushed rates back up to a nearly three-year high.
Related: US inflation rose 0.4% in October as price increases cooled and gas costs dipped

The 30-year mortgage rate, which is the most commonly used rate in home loans, is now hovering at about 7.18%, not far from its 2023 high of 7.79%. During the pandemic, average mortgage rates were just above 3%.

“Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Lawrence Yun, chief economist at the NAR. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”

Pending home sales, or the number of contracts that have been signed before closing, reached its lowest levels in the NAR’s history in September, the same month that the 30-year mortgage rate topped 7% for the first time in nearly two years.

Mortgage rates have been directly affected by interest rate changes by the US Federal Reserve, which in September hiked interest rates for the first time since 2023. Rates currently sit at a range of 3.75% to 4%.
The central bank is poised to raise rates again next month to combat heightened inflation, which went up more than expected in October.

Affordability and cost-of-living concerns played an outsized role in the midterm elections that gave Democrats control of Congress next year. According to the latest census data, growth in median rent across the US outpaced inflation. The home-ownership rate in the US has stagnated since 2021, according to the same data.

“I don’t think this is a new normal for home sales,” said Danielle Hale, chief economist at Realtor.com. “Instead, it reflects a perfect storm of an abrupt shift in the financial environment and large uncertainties in the pre-election period for both policy and the economy just as the housing market usually slows for the season.”

title_en: Seth Meyers on Trump’s midterms denial: ‘Watching you go through the motions is bumming me out’
excerpt_en: Late-night hosts discuss US president’s questioning of historic midterms defeat and his unpopular ‘triumphal arch’
body_en: Late-night hosts tore into Donald Trump going through the motions on election denial and his self-centered tribute for US Veterans Day.

Seth Meyers On Wednesday’s Late Night, Seth Meyers checked in with how Trump is processing Republicans’ historic defeat in the midterms, widely seen as a mass repudiation of his administration. The president initially seemed defeat, even depressed, in his acceptance of the results: “It’s just a point in time, it’s just the way it is,” he told Fox News last week.

“I’ve seen Trump angry, I’ve seen Trump tired, but I’ve never heard him so depressed,” Meyers laughed of that comment. “He’s going to do his next press conference in sweats, eating a pint of Haagen-Dazs.”
And “the sadder Trump gets, the more emboldened the press gets,” he added. “In fact, there’s one clip from a few days ago that really sums up the mood at the White House right now.”
Related: Jimmy Kimmel on Hegseth’s press conference amid impeachment attempt: ‘doozy of a performance’

The host then played a clip of Trump being asked by a reporter: “How does it feel being a loser, Mr President?” Trump did not answer, and instead walked quickly (by his standards) away from the press gaggle.

“Damn, he was out of there so fast, I thought he was gonna Mary Poppins out of frame,” Meyers joked. “It’s so funny to get asked what does it feel like to be a loser and then walk away alone in the rain. ‘How does it feel to be a loser? I’ll take my answer non-verbally.’”

“The point is, Trump seemed sad and resigned after the midterms, too resigned to gin up any fake outrage about the results,” Meyers added. “But on Monday, he picked himself up off the mat and got back to doing what he loves most: lying about elections.”
On Truth Social, Trump posted: “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong???”

“Does anyone believe this election was honest? Uh, yeah, you, two days ago!” Meyers mocked. “And now we’re blaming the machines again? What is this, a 2020-themed birthday party? Should I grab my N96 mask and throw on The Last Dance?”

“Seriously, dude, you don’t even believe your own bullshit,” he continued. “And watching you go through the motions is bumming me out. It’s like watching an old dog try to chase a car when every breath sounds like their last.”

Jimmy Kimmel And in Los Angeles, Jimmy Kimmel mocked Trump’s appearance at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday, ostensibly to observe Veterans Day in the US. “Typically, a president will show up and pay his respects to those who gave their lives to this country,” Kimmel explained. “Every Veterans Day, that’s how it goes. But this president saw it as a good opportunity to brag about all the money he claims to be raking in.”

In his speech, Trump bragged about taking “billions and billions of dollars” in oil from Venezuela, and added: “To the victor belongs the spoils, they used to say. But you can say it again with us, under this leadership.”
“Oh that’s great – then why is gas still $6 a gallon?” Kimmel retorted. “Maybe this victor is keeping the spoils for himself?”

Trump also boasted about his highly contested triumphal arch the “he’s building to honor himself,” said Kimmel. The arch, to be constructed next to Arlington, is now the subject of multiple lawsuits, though “they’re working very hard to claim that this arch is intended to honor the military.”

In fact, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle issued a statement this week claiming that the arch will serve as a “visual reminder of the noble sacrifices borne by so many American heroes throughout our 250-year history so we can enjoy our freedoms today”.

Kimmel offered a curt response: “Hey Dingle, your boss’s dumb vanity project is gonna cost us at least a hundred million dollars, maybe two hundred or three hundred million. And you know who could use that money? The VA [Veterans Administration], which is now in worse shape than ever, largely thanks to his big, beautiful budget cuts.”

“Donny Bonespurs and his sidekick Elon cut thousands of veteran jobs last year – 28,000 of those jobs were at the VA, including nurses, psychologists and social workers,” he added. “So unless that arch is filled with benefits for men and women who serve this country, maybe put a sock in it and go outside and play with the other kids.”

title_en: ‘Plenty of reasons for hope’: what 30 years of climate talks have achieved
excerpt_en: After 30 years of global climate talks, there has been more progress than you might think. A climate diplomacy expert explains why there’s still reason for hope.
body_en: Thousands of delegates, scientists and world leaders are gathered in Turkey for the latest United Nations climate summit, COP31. Their task is familiar: agree on how to cut greenhouse gas emissions and help countries cope with a warming planet.

But after more than three decades of negotiations, global emissions remain stubbornly high and the world is on course to overshoot the critical threshold of 1.5°C of warming. So have these annual summits actually achieved anything?
Dr Wesley Morgan, a climate diplomacy expert at UNSW Sydney, tells The Conversation Weekly podcast the answer is yes:
The Paris Agreement is a monumental diplomatic achievement.
Agreed in 2015, the treaty brought more than 190 countries together around shared climate goals. Morgan says it has helped shift the trajectory of global warming:
We were headed towards utter catastrophe. We’re still headed towards some very dire circumstances and more ambition is needed, but it is better than it would have been without this global agreement.
This year’s summit presents a particular diplomatic challenge for Australia because its climate and energy minister, Chris Bowen, is leading the negotiations.

Morgan says Australia can “tell a very positive story about what’s happening domestically in Australia”, including by pointing to significant strides in rooftop solar, which is now installed on one in three homes.
But Australia’s role as President of Negotiations at COP31 is controversial because Australia remains one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and gas.

In September, the federal government approved an expansion of BHP’s Saraji coal mine in Queensland, while authorities in New South Wales gave the green light for a major Hunter Valley coal mine to keep operating until 2045.
The negotiations also face a major setback following the Trump administration’s withdrawal in January from international climate cooperation.
Yet Morgan notes that no other country has followed the United States out of the talks.

Pressure from Europe and the Pacific European countries are expected to push for stronger commitments and stronger ambition from the COP 31 negotiations, following a summer of severe heatwaves and wildfires across the continent. “I think across Europe and in the UK, there’s a realisation that this is a clear and present danger now,” says Morgan.

He also points to the influence of Pacific island nations as evidence that smaller countries can shape global agreements. In 2015, The Republic of the Marshall Islands helped build the High Ambition Coalition, which was instrumental in securing the Paris Agreement and its 1.5°C goal.
For Pacific countries, Morgan says, that target is a matter of survival:
The rallying cry from the Pacific is 1.5 to stay alive.
One possible outcome from COP31 is a new global electrification target dubbed “35 by 35”: meeting 35% of the world’s final energy demand with electricity by 2035.
Morgan sees it as another step towards economies powered by clean energy – and despite the setbacks, he insists the transition is already underway:
There’s plenty of reasons for hope as well as reasons for despair.
Wesley Morgan is a fellow at the Climate Council of Australia.

title_en: European survey reveals 900m galaxies – and possibly secrets of ‘dark universe’
excerpt_en: Unprecedented view of cosmos provided by Euclid mission throws up many more cases of gravitational lensing
body_en: A mission to create the largest ever 3D map of the universe has revealed more than 900m galaxies in its first major data release together with about 15,000 potential cases of a phenomenon that could help unlock the secrets of the “dark universe”.
Launched in July 2023, the European Space Agency’s Euclid mission promised to create the largest cosmic map ever made, encompassing a third of the sky and more than 10bn years of cosmic history.
The goal is to shed light on two of the biggest mysteries in the universe: the nature of dark energy and dark matter. These are thought to make up about 70% and 25% of the universe respectively.

Prof Andy Taylor, of the University of Edinburgh, who leads the UK science ground segment for the mission, said while there were bigger surveys, none had the detail and the information content of Euclid. By contrast the Hubble telescope has produced images of incredible resolution, but does not cover as large an area of the sky.
“The technological leap that’s Euclid is that we can keep that high resolution, but now we can basically map huge volumes of the sky, huge volumes of the universe,” Taylor said.
Now, the first major Euclid data release has landed, offering researchers an unprecedented view of the cosmos. “It’s the biggest high-resolution image of the universe we’ve ever had,” Taylor said.

Covering about 14% of the total area of sky that will be mapped by Euclid, the newly released data captures over 900m galaxies as well more than 60m potential quasars: blazing objects at the centre of distant galaxies, powered by supermassive black holes.
Related: Scientists hail ‘avalanche of discoveries’ from Euclid space telescope

It also includes a tranche of candidates for what was previously considered a rare phenomenon: strong gravitational lensing. This is a magnification effect that occurs when one galaxy, often embedded in a galaxy cluster, sits in front of another, distant galaxy.

As Taylor notes, Einstein predicted the gravitational influence of the foreground galaxy would distort space-time, bending the light from the background galaxy and creating the appearance of bright arcs or rings. Crucially, the effect is significantly boosted by the presence of dark matter, which increases the mass and hence gravitational influence of a galaxy.

Taylor said that by studying strong gravitational lensing, scientists may be able to rule out different theories on the nature of dark matter. That is because the lensing is influenced by how this mysterious substance is distributed in a galaxy – that itself depends on its properties.

Stephen Serjeant, a professor of astronomy at the Open University, agreed. “With strong gravitational lensing, you find out how the dark matter is clumping and that’s very diagnostic of the type of matter that it is, because different types of matter can clump in very different ways,” he said.

“So if you’re looking for where the next breakthrough will be in the properties of dark matter and what dark matter actually is, there’s a good chance – I can’t say it’s certain – but there’s a good chance it might come from strong gravitational lensing.”

Taylor noted that while experts previously knew of about 1,000 cases of strong gravitational lensing, the Euclid data contains about 15,000 probable cases, with an estimated 170,000 expected to be discovered by the end of the mission.
Related: First section of Euclid space telescope’s map of the universe revealed

A further release of data was expected to land next summer, Taylor added, which will include results on both the distribution of galaxies as well as weak gravitational lensing – subtle distortions in distant objects by dark matter in the foreground.

“We can use that pattern of distortions to actually make a map of where all the dark matter is in the universe,” said Taylor, adding that scientists could then work out its statistical properties and compare the results with different theories. “Depending on the type of dark matter, the type of dark energy, we’re expecting to see slightly different patterns on the sky.”
And with Euclid generating ever-more data, Taylor noted there was plenty to explore.

“It’s opening up that high resolution of the whole sky, the whole universe. So it just means there are plenty of objects that we’ll never have seen before, plenty of research phenomena,” he said. “No human eyeball is able to look at all of the Euclid data any more. It’s now too big.”

title_en: What lurks ‘Below’ Newfoundland waters? A marine biologist explains the science behind the show
excerpt_en: While Below may have some things wrong — giant squid probably aren’t vindictive, for example — a Newfoundland ocean sciences expert praises the Netflix show for stoking an interest in the deep sea.
body_en: Tokyo then, St. John's now? A giant squid attacks a bait squid off the coast of Tokyo in 2006. (Tsunemi Kubodera/National Science Museum of Japan), CC BY When I learned that Netflix planned to film the miniseries Below, about a sea monster terrorizing a Newfoundland outport, I thought to myself: “THIS I’ve gotta see!”

First, the series showcases coastal Newfoundland, where I was raised and live. Second, I have studied ocean life in the island’s waters for most of my career. Third, it features the marine lab where I work, the Oceans Sciences Centre. And fourth, it stars a giant squid(-ish) animal (sorry Josh Hartnett).
Giant squid have a special place in Newfoundland folklore and science, from early encounters with fishermen to some of the first scientific evidence of their existence.

Unveiling the giant squid One key player in this history was the Irish clergyman Moses Harvey, who moved to Newfoundland in 1852 and undertook natural history research in what was then a British colony.

Harvey’s research included revealing the existence of giant squid to the world based on a specimen that washed ashore. Fishermen had brought it to him to photograph and communicate to the science community in London.

Arms, tentacles and head (buccal region, including beak visible) of a giant squid from Logy Bay, Newfoundland, photographed draped over Moses Harvey’s sponge bath in November 1873. (Variously attributed to John Maunder, Moses Harvey and Messrs. McKenny and Parsons) Fast forward to the 1960s, when the founding director of the Ocean Sciences Centre, Fred Aldrich, joined the faculty at Memorial University and soon focused his career on pursuing giant squid.
Although Aldrich tried to catch a living specimen, he only obtained squid that washed up on beaches.

Newfoundland is one of the global hotspots where giant squid appear more frequently, every 30 years or so (New Zealand is another, attesting to giant squid affinity for cooler waters). Below ‘s arrival roughly coincides with one of those cycles.
The Rooms provincial museum in St. John’s displays a preserved version of one of these amazing animals.

Giant squid: Not known to be vindictive Early in the series, we meet an (oddly) barefooted marine biologist walking through the hallways of the marine lab. This scene earned a loud “ewww” from my graduate students on the grounds of hygiene as well as occupational health and safety.

The biologist turns out to be the expert on giant squid and the voice of sanity when fishermen, the military and a local developer all pursue the creature (nicknamed “Mudder” by the locals, foreshadowing why she is attacking the community) with bloodlust.

This marine biologist also provides impromptu medical expertise when residents fall ill from drinking ice water tainted by the animal. (Side note, DO NOT entrust your local marine biologist with urgent medical needs — we are not that type of doctor!)

I could join the Facebook crowd quibbling about who got the Newfoundland accents right and who missed the mark. Or I could ask why the Coast Guard would fully abandon people living on a small, isolated island in crisis.
But Below generally did a good job on the science. The biology of the animal was reasonably plausible, including its swimming skills and even its ability to survive in ice.

As a (likely necessary) stretch, I thought the intellectual prowess and directed vindictiveness of the squid in the series pushed the limits of credibility, although researchers have documented some impressive abilities in cephalopods (of which giant squid are members). Still, it was a good effort to maintain scientific plausibility and fun to see marine biota as the star attraction.

Historical accuracy I took a course in marine invertebrates from Aldrich when I was an undergraduate in the early 1980s. Although he was in the late stages of his career, his enthusiasm for giant squid was still evident in his lectures.

He would have loved to have seen the first live footage of giant squid in the wild collected just 20 years ago by Japanese scientists, and I think he would have enjoyed watching Below and he’d be happy I’m writing about it.

I certainly enjoyed watching Below, not just because of the Newfoundland setting but because it seemed entirely appropriate for the story, which was in some ways a homage to Newfoundland and its ocean history.
The plot weaved in the innate capacity of local fishers to adapt and work together to solve challenges (who can “put the arse back in a cat,” as locals would say).

It addressed the collapse of the northern cod fishery that threw some 37,000 Newfoundlanders out of work. And it began with a striking scene about the government’s resettlement of more than 28,000 residents of many small coastal communities to larger centres in the 1950s and '60s.

It also captured the general mistrust of government in outport communities. My CFA (come from away) graduate students also appreciated seeing the “Screeching In” ceremony, and the real sense of Newfoundland conveyed by the series.
Read more: The trauma caused by resettlement in Newfoundland and Labrador must be acknowledged

title_en: “We Have No One”: How Trump’s Dismantling of the VA Left a Veterans Hospital in Crisis
excerpt_en: The post “We Have No One”: How Trump’s Dismantling of the VA Left a Veterans Hospital in Crisis appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Hokyoung Kim for ProPublica John Falchetto was a survivor. In Vietnam, his river gunboat came under devastating rocket fire. He was the only one to make it out alive. But this February, Falchetto, who had just turned 80, began to have piercing stomach pains. He was in distress for days. Finally, Falchetto went to the VA hospital in East Orange, New Jersey.

A CT scan of Falchetto’s abdomen suggested his appendix had not only burst, but that it was gangrenous. His gut was so filled with bacteria and pus that tissue was dying. Doctors wrote that he needed surgery immediately.

But that night, the hospital’s operating room was closed. Months earlier, the ventilation system had malfunctioned, and the repair team was short-staffed. So Falchetto lay there, his life in the balance, for seven hours.
This was not normal. But nothing had been normal at East Orange since President Donald Trump returned to office last year and set his sights on the VA.

The behemoth agency, which traces its roots to the Civil War, is both the country’s largest healthcare system and one of its most effective. It provides 9 million veterans what is essentially socialized medicine, often for free, under the cover of the American flag. The doctors, nurses and other staff are employed by the government.

Despite the occasional scandal and persistent short-staffing, studies have shown that the VA — where the doctors coordinate with one another and have deep expertise on veterans’ needs — has better outcomes than private care.

But in his second term, Trump has moved aggressively to upend this system, embracing a decades-long conservative campaig n to effectively kneecap the VA’s government-run healthcare and shift veterans toward private doctors and hospitals.

Under Trump, the VA has increasingly acted like an insurer, paying doctors in the community for vets’ care. This, the reasoning went, would allow the government to cut thousands of needless bureaucrats while giving veterans more choices if the VA can’t provide the care.
Do You Know About Staffing Shortages at a VA Hospital? Tell Me About Them. Have you seen setbacks in care amid the changes at the Department of Veterans Affairs? ProPublica wants to hear from you.
Share Your Experience “We love our veterans,” Trump said during an Oval Office photo op shortly after his inauguration. “We are going to take good care of them.”

Days after that pronouncement, a memo leaked showing the administration was considering sweeping job cuts at the agency. “Things need to change,” warned Doug Collins, Trump’s new VA secretary, in a video message to staff.
After pushback from vets groups and others, the administration retreated from its threat of mass layoffs. But it found another, less attention-getting way to shrink the VA.
If Trump’s appointees couldn’t lay off employees, they would make work conditions so untenable that staffers would leave on their own.

The administration canceled the contracts of the agency’s unions — citing national security concerns. They ordered remote staffers back to the office. Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency demanded employees report what they had accomplished each week. And the administration offered staffers early retirement packages and other incentives to quit.
Throughout it all, the VA’s leadership said front-line medical workers would be immune from any cuts. But amid the upheaval, many left anyway.

Six months after Trump entered the White House, the VA had 3,800 fewer doctors, nurses and other “mission critical” staff than it did at the start of his term, according to the department’s own data. While the losses made up a small percentage of overall employees, the drop compounded longstanding shortages — and contrasted sharply with a hiring spree under President Joe Biden that had begun to address them. Many of the front-line workers who quit in Trump’s early days have never been replaced. Instead, the VA has eliminated thousands of open positions, including doctors, nurses and other providers.

The administration has denied that it is hurting veterans’ care. “There’s actually an excitement about what’s going on,” said Collins, a former personal lawyer for Trump, in congressional testimony this spring. A spokesperson said the eliminated jobs for healthcare providers were simply “not needed.”

That is not what we have found. Over months of reporting, ProPublica has watched the East Orange VA Medical Center — a typical agency facility — spiral downward. The hospital and its affiliated facilities in New Jersey lost nearly a tenth of the staff they had when Trump took office.

Over the past two years, a VA watchdog report shows, the number of roles with “ severe shortages ” in East Orange has tripled, from around 30 to roughly 90. Among them: oncologists, radiologists, surgeons, cardiologists, anesthesiologists, critical care doctors, nurses, mechanics, cleaners — nearly every job that makes a hospital run.
“It’s scary,” one East Orange administrator said in a meeting this year. “We have no one.”

It’s not just there. According to the VA’s watchdog, nearly all VA hospitals — 97% — reported having severe shortages of doctors. (The agency argues that the report — titled in part, “Staffing Shortages” — is simply about shortages of candidates and not actual staffing.)

The exodus of healthcare providers has increasingly forced veterans into the private care program — called Community Care — that the Trump administration has pushed. Amid soaring caseloads there and what a government report describes as “insufficient staffing,” many vets have been facing interminable waits.
